**Title:** MetCool ACS: study protocol for a multicentre quasi-randomised trial of metformin in patients without diabetes after acute coronary syndrome in Poland.

**Authors:** Edyta Sutkowska, Piotr Kwiatkowski, Renata Mazur, Grzegorz Gielerak

**Journal:** BMJ open
**Publication Date:** 2026-10-23

Despite advances in coronary intervention and secondary prevention, patients without diabetes who experience acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remain at elevated cardiovascular risk. Metformin has pleiotropic cardiovascular effects beyond glucose lowering, but its role after ACS in people without diabetes is uncertain.

MetCool ACS is a multicentre, prospective, quasi-randomised, open-label trial enrolling 1000 adults without diabetes hospitalised for ACS and treated with successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stent implantation. Allocation is determined by the second digit of the Polish national identification number: even digits allocate to metformin and odd digits to standard care (allocation 1:1). Participants allocated to metformin will receive dose-escalated therapy to 850 mg three times a day (2550 mg/day) for 24 months, followed by 6 months of post-treatment follow-up (total 30 months). The primary endpoint is unplanned coronary revascularisation (PCI or coronary artery bypass grafting) within 30 months after the index ACS-related revascularisation. Secondary endpoints include cardiac death, all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke and safety outcomes. Time-to-event outcomes will be analysed using appropriate survival analysis methods, including Kaplan-Meier estimates, log-rank testing and Cox proportional hazards models, with competing-risk methods applied where appropriate. Detailed statistical methods will be prespecified in the statistical analysis plan. Protocol version: 3.1/2023 (10 January 2023).

The study was approved by the Bioethics Committee at the Military Institute of Medicine (Resolution 55/WIM/2020; 18 November 2020) and the Bioethics Committee at the Military Chamber of Physicians (Resolution 31/23; 27 October 2023). All participants provide written informed consent. Results will be disseminated primarily through peer-reviewed publication and scientific meetings. The trial is covered by clinical trial insurance, including coverage for potential claims arising from harm related to participation in the trial. Any compensation for trial-related harm will be provided in accordance with applicable regulations and the terms and conditions of the insurance policy.

EudraCT 2020-004962-21; EU CT 2024-516589-13-00; NCT05305898.

Keywords: Coronary heart disease, Coronary intervention, CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY, Drug Therapy

Large, multicentre prospective design across major interventional cardiology centres in Poland.

Focus on post-acute coronary syndrome patients without diabetes, allowing assessment of non-glycaemic effects of metformin.

Long follow-up (30 months) with standardised monitoring of cardiac function and ischaemia.

Quasi-random allocation using Polish national identification number digit may risk baseline imbalance.

Open-label design without placebo may introduce performance or detection bias, particularly because the diagnostic pathway leading to revascularisation may be influenced by clinical assessment.

Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) encompasses unstable angina, non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (MI) and ST-segment elevation MI. Despite prompt revascularisation and contemporary secondary prevention, recurrent events and repeat revascularisation remain clinically important in patients without diabetes.

Restenosis and other causes of repeat coronary intervention are multifactorial and include inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress and thrombosis-related pathways.1–5 Metabolic mechanisms may also contribute independent of baseline glycaemia.

Metformin is a biguanide widely used to treat type 2 diabetes. In addition to glycaemic effects, metformin influences endothelial function, inflammation, platelet activity and cellular bioenergetics.6
7 The UK Prospective Diabetes Study demonstrated cardiovascular benefits of metformin in patients with type 2 diabetes, suggesting potential cardioprotective effects beyond glycaemic control.8
9 However, long-term follow-up of the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study did not demonstrate a reduction in major cardiovascular events, although attenuation of coronary atherosclerosis was observed in men with prediabetes.10
11 Several trials evaluating metformin in people without diabetes (MetCAB, CAMERA and GIPS-III) also failed to demonstrate clear clinical benefit but were limited by relatively short treatment duration, low metformin doses and evaluation in stable rather than acute ischaemic settings.12–16

Accordingly, MetCool ACS will test whether full-dose metformin, initiated after successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for ACS, reduces the need for unplanned coronary revascularisation in adults without diabetes.

To evaluate whether metformin reduces the incidence of unplanned coronary revascularisation (PCI or coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)) within 30 months after successful index ACS-related revascularisation in adults without diabetes.

To compare cardiac death, all-cause death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke and safety outcomes between groups over 30 months.

MetCool ACS is a multicentre, prospective, quasi-randomised, open-label clinical trial with a fixed sample size. The open-label design was chosen because the trial was designed as an investigator-initiated pragmatic study intended to reflect routine clinical practice. Although the absence of placebo and blinding may introduce performance and detection bias, the primary endpoint consists of clinically relevant coronary revascularisation procedures (PCI or CABG), which are objective events documented according to predefined clinical criteria. The potential influence of clinical assessment on the diagnostic pathway leading to revascularisation is acknowledged as a limitation of the study.

It is conducted in Poland, led by the Military Institute of Medicine in Warsaw, with participating interventional cardiology centres from the Scanmed group and the Multispecialty Provincial Hospital in Gorzow Wielkopolski. The lead investigator at each site must be a physician with a cardiology specialty. An example of the participant informed consent form is provided as online supplemental file 1. Written informed consent will be obtained by the investigator responsible for the participant at each participating site.

ACS defined according to current European Society of Cardiology guidance, treated with PCI and drug-eluting stent implantation.

Able to attend scheduled follow-up visits.

Uncomplicated in-hospital course of ACS, as assessed by the treating physician.

No prior diagnosis of diabetes and no hypoglycaemic therapy within 6 months before hospitalisation.

Glycated hemoglobin <6.5% during index hospitalisation.

Written informed consent.

Significant valvular heart disease on echocardiography.

New York Heart Association (NYHA) class IV during hospitalisation.

Chronic kidney disease with estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min/1.73 m² (Modification of Diet in Renal Disease).

Alanine aminotransferase >3× upper limit of normal.

Serious comorbidity with life expectancy <2.5 years, as assessed by the attending physician.

Gastrointestinal disease that may cause metformin intolerance (eg, inflammatory bowel disease, severe gastro-oesophageal reflux disease).

Known adherence concerns (eg, dementia, severe psychiatric disorder, problematic travel distance, alcohol dependence).

Known hypersensitivity to metformin.

Pregnancy or breastfeeding.

Participation in another clinical trial.

Allocation is determined by the second digit of the PESEL (Polish national identification number): even digits allocate to metformin and odd digits allocate to standard care. Allocation is performed by investigators independent of the recruiting site and cannot be altered. Although the allocation procedure is based on a predefined rule independent of clinical characteristics and investigator decisions, it does not provide full allocation concealment. Baseline characteristics will therefore be compared between treatment groups to evaluate the effectiveness of the allocation procedure and to identify any potential imbalance.

Participants allocated to metformin will start treatment within 14 days after PCI. The lead investigator at each site will administer the therapy. Doses will be escalated over 6 weeks to a target of 850 mg three times a day (2550 mg/day) and continued for 24 months. If intolerance occurs, the dose may be reduced to the previously tolerated dose. Persistent intolerance at the minimum dose (500 mg once daily) will result in discontinuation of metformin, but participants will remain in follow-up according to their original treatment allocation. Other reasons for treatment discontinuation or withdrawal may include withdrawal of consent, medical contraindications, clinically significant adverse events, suspected interaction with other medication, inability to continue study participation, non-adherence, or major protocol deviations. No replacement of participants withdrawn from the study is planned. Participants who discontinue study treatment will remain eligible for outcome follow-up whenever possible and will be included in the intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis according to their original allocation.

Participants allocated to standard care will receive guideline-based management for acute and chronic coronary syndromes. No placebo will be used. Use of oral or parenteral glucose-lowering agents is not permitted during the trial. However, if an SGLT2 inhibitor becomes clinically indicated during the study for a cardiovascular or renal indication, its initiation will not constitute a reason for withdrawal from the trial. Such treatment will be documented, and participants will remain in the study and will be analysed according to their original treatment allocation. In contrast, patients receiving an SGLT2 inhibitor before enrolment are not eligible for inclusion. Patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists or dual agonists prior to study enrolment will also not be eligible for inclusion. If treatment with these agents is proposed during a participant’s study participation, the case will be considered individually to determine whether the participant may remain in the study. Participants are informed about their participation in the study and instructed to inform the investigator before initiating any new therapy that may have glucose-lowering effects.

Participants may withdraw consent at any time without providing a reason. Treatment may also be discontinued for safety reasons, clinically relevant adverse events, medical contraindications, suspected drug interactions, non-adherence or other circumstances preventing safe continuation. Participants withdrawn from treatment will not be replaced and, where possible, will continue to be followed for study outcomes.

Screening includes informed consent. Baseline assessments include clinical examination, ECG, echocardiography and laboratory testing. Follow-up visits are scheduled at 3, 7, 12, 24 and 30 months after allocation, including symptom assessment (Canadian Cardiovascular Society and NYHA class), ECG, echocardiography and laboratory testing according to the study schedule. Participants who discontinue the study medication or are unable to attend scheduled visits will be followed for clinical outcomes whenever feasible, and the date of their last adequate assessment will be recorded for survival analyses.

Clinical data are recorded in a study-specific electronic case report form developed within the REDCap data capture platform and are centrally managed by the Military Institute of Medicine—National Research Institute (WIM) in Warsaw, with data quality monitored through source data verification, completeness and consistency checks, and resolution of data queries by an independent Contract Research Organisation (CRO).

In participants with worsening symptoms suggestive of chronic coronary syndrome, single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) will be performed according to predefined clinical criteria. If significant ischaemia (>10%) is detected, coronary angiography and subsequent treatment will follow contemporary guidance and predefined study criteria. The indication for further ischaemia testing and subsequent coronary angiography or revascularisation will be assessed by the investigator responsible for the participant at the participating centre. In cases of uncertainty regarding the classification of a potential primary endpoint event, the case may be discussed with the senior investigator at the participating centre and, if necessary, with the principal investigator. Because the decision to initiate further ischaemia testing may be influenced by clinical assessment, variation in diagnostic and revascularisation practices across centres and investigators cannot be completely excluded and is acknowledged as a potential source of ascertainment bias.

All participants will undergo SPECT at the final visit (30 months). Results from tests conducted up to 21 days before a visit may be used.

Unplanned coronary revascularisation (PCI or CABG) occurring within 30 months after the index ACS-related revascularisation. Because eligibility requires complete and successful revascularisation of the index ACS event before enrolment, any subsequent coronary revascularisation during follow-up is considered unplanned for the purpose of the primary endpoint, provided that the prespecified endpoint criteria are fulfilled. Staged or incomplete revascularisation related to the index ACS event is completed before enrolment and is therefore not considered a primary endpoint event.

Cardiac death within 30 months.

All-cause death within 30 months.

Non-fatal MI within 30 months.

Non-fatal stroke within 30 months.

Safety outcomes, assessed by the proportion and types of adverse events and serious adverse events.

Participants will be monitored systematically throughout the study for treatment tolerance, vital signs, laboratory values and adverse events, including at scheduled follow-up visits. Adverse events will be assessed based on participant reports, clinical assessment, vital signs and laboratory findings. Serious adverse events will be identified and reported in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements and International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use – Good Clinical Practice definitions. Serious adverse events will be reported to the sponsor and the CRO within 24 hours, with further reporting timelines aligned with applicable regulations. Suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions will be reported to the relevant regulatory authorities by the CRO.

The sample size calculation specified in the study protocol indicated that 323 participants per group were required under the prespecified assumptions, using a two-sided significance level of 0.05 and 80% statistical power. The calculation was based on a 30-month primary endpoint event rate of 20% in the control group, a 20% relative risk reduction and an HR of 0.75.

The sample size was then increased by 50% to account for potential attrition, resulting in 485 participants per group (323×1.50=484.5, rounded to 485). This corresponded to 970 participants overall and the planned recruitment target was subsequently rounded to 1000 participants.

The assumed treatment effect was based on indirect evidence from studies of metformin in populations with type 2 diabetes or prediabetes, as direct randomised evidence for a reduction in cardiovascular events with metformin in non-diabetic patients after ACS is lacking. Therefore, the assumed treatment effect should be interpreted as a prespecified design assumption informed by indirect evidence rather than as an evidence-based estimate of treatment efficacy in this specific population.

The primary analysis will be conducted according to the ITT principle. All participants will be analysed according to their original treatment allocation, regardless of treatment adherence, treatment discontinuation or protocol deviations. Participants who discontinue study treatment but consent to continued follow-up will remain under observation and will be included in the primary analysis according to their original allocation. No replacement of participants withdrawn from the study is planned.

Time-to-event outcomes will be analysed using appropriate survival analysis methods. Kaplan-Meier estimates, log-rank testing and Cox proportional hazards models will be used as appropriate. In the presence of competing events, particularly death before occurrence of the primary endpoint, cumulative incidence functions and appropriate competing-risk regression methods will be considered.

A per-protocol analysis will be performed as a sensitivity analysis and will include participants meeting the prespecified criteria for adherence to the study protocol. Additional sensitivity analyses may be performed as specified in the statistical analysis plan (SAP).

No imputation of missing outcome data is planned for the primary or secondary time-to-event endpoints. Participants without a documented event will be censored at the end of the available follow-up or at the date of the last adequate assessment, according to predefined censoring rules, as applicable.

Subgroup analyses were not prespecified in the study protocol. Any exploratory subgroup or sensitivity analyses will be defined in the SAP before database lock and unblinding.

The primary endpoint will be considered the sole confirmatory endpoint. Secondary endpoints will be analysed as supportive and exploratory outcomes; no formal adjustment for multiplicity is planned for secondary endpoint analyses.

The detailed statistical methodology, including the handling of competing risks, treatment discontinuation, protocol deviations, adherence, censoring and sensitivity analyses, will be specified in the SAP, which will be finalised before database lock and unblinding.
